# The Light-Leak

The camera arrived in a shoebox lined with newspaper from 1987. My neighbor Mrs. Okonkwo handed it over the fence like she was passing me a sleeping infant.

"It was my husband's. A Yashica Mat-124G. Twin-lens reflex. He photographed every block party from 1974 until his hands got too shaky." She paused. "You look down into it, not through it. You'll see."

I'd volunteered to document the Maple Street centennial celebration because I was the only person on the block who owned a tripod, and because I'd once mentioned at a potluck that I "liked photography," which was technically true—I liked the idea of it, the way I liked the idea of learning Italian. I'd taken maybe forty photos in the last year, all on my phone, all forgettable.

The Yashica was heavier than I expected, all metal and leatherette, smelling faintly of machine oil and decades. I loaded the 120 film Mrs. Okonkwo had ordered specially—she'd bought six rolls, an act of faith that made my stomach tighten. Twelve exposures per roll. Twelve.
